Sober
sō´ber
adj. (self-controlled, clear-minded; rendering Greek nepho and sophron)
From Latin sobrius, not drunk. The New Testament keeps the literal sense but leans on the figurative: a mind not intoxicated by anything.

Biblical Definition

Sober means clear-headed and self-controlled. Peter attaches it to watchfulness in the presence of a predator: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour” (1Pe 5:8), and to prayer itself — “be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer” (1Pe 4:7). Paul makes it eschatological: “let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love” (1Th 5:8). It is required of overseers and of aged men alike (Tit 2:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sober as temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; not intoxicated; and as having the regular exercise of cool dispassionate reason.

expand to see more

SOBER, a. Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; habitually temperate.

2. Not intoxicated or overpowered by spirituous liquors; not drunken.

3. Not mad or insane; having the regular exercise of cool dispassionate reason.

4. Regular; calm; not under the influence of passion; not heated or wild.

Key Scripture

1Pe 5:8 — "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:"

1Pe 4:7 — "But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer."

1Th 5:8 — "But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation."

Tit 2:2 — "That the aged men be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience."

Modern Corruption

Sobriety is filed as an abstinence issue only, when the New Testament aims it at every intoxicant of the mind — outrage, appetite, spectacle, and the endless feed.

expand to see more

Peter's pairing tells us what sobriety is for: be sober, be vigilant, because a lion is hunting. A drunk man is not primarily immoral; he is unable to perceive danger accurately or respond to it quickly, and that incapacity is the point of the metaphor. Anything that leaves a Christian slow to notice temptation, dulled to conscience, and reactive rather than watchful has done the work of drink, whatever it is called.

The connection to prayer in 1 Peter 4:7 is the one most often missed. Be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer — a scattered, over-stimulated mind cannot pray, and no amount of sincerity compensates. Much of what Christians diagnose as a prayer problem is a sobriety problem, and the remedy is not more resolve at the moment of prayer but fewer intoxicants during the day.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek nepho (G3525), to be sober, unintoxicated, watchful; sophron (G4998), sound-minded — the two strands of the word in the epistles.

expand to see more

Greek nepho (G3525) — to be sober, watchful; 1 Peter 1:13, 4:7, 5:8, 1 Thessalonians 5:6.

Greek sophron (G4998) — of sound mind, discreet; Titus 2:2, 1 Timothy 3:2.

Greek sophroneo (G4993) — to think soberly; Romans 12:3, not to think more highly than he ought.

Usage

"“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil…” — sobriety is threat-perception."

"“Be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer” — a dulled mind cannot pray."

"“Let us, who are of the day, be sober” — clear-headedness as an eschatological posture."
